routes.description: Establish that meaningful proximity requires a chemically specified and experimentally credible account of producing, preserving, organizing, and integrating the components of first life, and that current work has not met that burden.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the unresolved requirements for molecular synthesis, stereochemistry, sequencing, assembly, and cellular organization outweigh appeals to abstract possibility, large opportunity spaces, elapsed time, or limited directional clues.

motionBridge.description: Show that current science lacks a sufficiently complete and credible chemical pathway to count as meaningfully close to explaining first life.

centralBridges.description: Specify the multiple molecular classes and integrated organizational steps that an origin account must explain.
Require probability and possibility claims to engage the cumulative chemistry of production, preservation, and assembly.
Determine whether experimental advances approach the explanatory target or whether growing knowledge of complexity makes that target more remote.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for whether long timescales preserve useful intermediates or instead amplify decomposition and side reactions.
Use unresolved features of cellular organization to clarify why possessing molecular components may not explain the transition to life.

routes.description: Establish that incomplete mechanistic understanding can coexist with limited scientific clues and a defensible agnostic position when the probability, opportunity space, recurrence, and recoverability of natural abiogenesis remain unresolved.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if current evidence supplies some burden-relevant direction while leaving neither natural emergence nor alternatives demonstrated or excluded, so present remoteness does not warrant treating the scientific search as devoid of explanatory contact.

motionBridge.description: Show that limited empirical or theoretical clues provide meaningful explanatory contact while still requiring agnosticism about a complete origin account.

centralBridges.description: Relate a finite natural-origin probability to the universe's unknown number of opportunities without claiming that either quantity is presently measurable.
Distinguish possessing limited directional clues from possessing a complete, demonstrated mechanism.
Identify observations, including demonstrably independent origins, that could materially change the assessment of natural abiogenesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Allow for conceptual breakthroughs that could change the pace of progress despite prolonged present confusion.
Consider whether an extraordinarily rare and unrepeatable origin could remain partly inaccessible to scientific reconstruction.

sections.title: Chemical Production, Preservation, and Cellular Assembly
sections.rationale: This issue defines the principal explanatory burden by asking what molecular classes, reaction sequences, stability conditions, and organizational steps must be accounted for before first life has a credible chemical pathway.

sections.title: Nonzero Probability and Cosmic Opportunity
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether finite reaction probabilities and an immense opportunity space support agnosticism or remain too abstract without accounting for the many required synthesis and assembly steps.

sections.title: Limited Clues and Distance from an Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the motion's meaningfully-close standard by distinguishing partial directional knowledge from a complete account and by asking whether the explanatory target is approaching or receding.

sections.title: Independent Origins as an Empirical Test
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether independently arisen extraterrestrial life would reveal that abiogenesis is naturally accessible, and whether recurrence alone would illuminate the underlying mechanism.

sections.title: Timescales, Breakthroughs, and Scientific Recoverability
sections.rationale: This issue brings together whether time aids or degrades prebiotic chemistry, whether progress may arrive discontinuously, and whether a singular rare event could be reconstructed by science at all.
